description: We are team "S I N G U L A R I T Y"
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app that compares up to three Moon landing sites on the same date and answers two questions for each one: is the Sun above this site's real skyline (power), and is Earth in view (direct radio contact)? It draws each site's terrain in 3D from NASA elevation maps, lit at the true Sun angle from JPL Horizons, and lays all sites on one 30-day timeline. A planner picks a 2, 7 or 14-day mission and the app marks each site Go, Marginal or No-go, then shows what a launch delay of 6 hours or 1 day does to that verdict. On 19 Oct 2027, 11 of the 13 Artemis III candidate regions are Go for a 2-day mission; if the launch slips 3 days, only 4 still are. Existing tools hold this data across several screens. This one shows it on one screen, in plain words, and every number on it is checked against JPL Horizons and NASA's own sunlight map.
details:
What it does

Pick up to three sites: from 25 built-in candidate sites, by any coordinates you type, or by any point you click on the 3D Moon. Each site gets a column:

- Its terrain in 3D, lit at the true Sun angle, with small Sun and Earth markers. Hover to read each body's height above level ground and the time until it sets.

- A sky chart (one click): the site's real skyline, with the paths of the Sun and Earth over the next 30 days drawn against it.

- A verdict in plain words, such as "Go for 2.5 days", "Dark now, next 4 Nov" or "Sun sets in 11.7 days".

- A launch-delay line under the verdict: what the verdict becomes if the launch is 6 hours, 1 day or 3 days late.

Go means the Sun is above the skyline and Earth is in view now, and both stay up for longer than the mission. Marginal means both are up now but one sets before the mission ends. No-go means the Sun is below the skyline or Earth is out of view.

At the 13 Artemis III regions and at Apollo 11, a rover mode lets you drive on NASA's 5 m maps (2 m at Apollo 11) and see the Sun and Earth from the ground.

The download button saves the 30 days as a CSV table (Sun and Earth elevation and azimuth, skyline height and the verdict, every hour, for every site). The address bar always holds a link to the current view, so a planner can send the exact comparison to a colleague.

How it works

1. Sun and Earth positions: we downloaded the Sun and Earth directions for each site every 6 hours from 1 Jan 2023 to 5 Mar 2031 from JPL Horizons (DE441) and interpolate between them in the browser. Earth's libration (its wobble in the lunar sky) and the Moon's orbit are inside these positions, so the app does not approximate either.

2. Skylines: for each built-in site we cast rays from 2 m above the ground in 1,440 directions (every 0.25°) out to 300 km. Each ray reads the finest NASA map that covers it: the 5 m shape-from-shading maps near the landing point, then the LOLA 80 m polar map, then a 625 m LOLA grid. Each ray follows the curved surface of the Moon. The Moon has no air, so there is no refraction: the skyline is terrain and the edge of the sphere, nothing else.

3. Up or down: the Sun counts as up when its centre is above the skyline height in its direction; Earth counts as in view the same way. The app samples every hour and finds each rise and set time to the minute.

4. Rendering: Three.js draws the terrain from the same NASA height maps and lights it from the true Sun direction with real-time shadows. Nothing is drawn when nothing changes, so the page stays cool on a weak laptop.

The landing point inside each Artemis III region is the sunniest 60 m spot in NASA's sunlight map whose ground within 50 m is at least 95% under 8° of slope on the 5 m map. Past landings use the lander positions published by LROC and NASA's NSSDC.

What it shows that a single site cannot

Small moves and short delays change everything at the south pole. Connecting Ridge and Connecting Ridge Extension are 21 km apart: one is in sunlight 87% of the time, the other 68%. On 19 Oct 2027 at 06:00 UTC, 11 of the 13 Artemis III regions are Go for a 2-day mission. Three days later, only 4 are (Haworth, Nobile Rim 1, Leibnitz Beta Plateau and Malapert Massif). The other 9 lose Earth or the Sun before the mission ends. The app shows this in one view.

How accurate is it

Sun and Earth elevation and azimuth at all 25 sites on 15 dates from 2023 to 2030, against JPL Horizons (allowed error 0.01°). Plus every rise and set time over two lunar days at 4 polar sites (allowed error 1% of the time until it). => 802 of 802 PASS. Largest direction error 0.000031°. Largest rise or set error 0.085% of the time until it.

Each south pole site's share of time in sunlight against NASA's own sunlight map (Mazarico et al. 2011), allowed gap 5 percentage points. => 13 of 14 PASS. de Gerlache-Kocher Massif is 6.2 points over. (Reason Below)

Rover physics, and that each 5 m and 2 m map lines up with the coarser LOLA map around it. => 34 of 34 PASS. Average height offset 1.3 m or less.

Why Kocher is 6.2 points off: NASA's map gives one 60 m pixel at ground level; the app gives one 5 m point seen from 2 m up. NASA's own neighbouring pixels on this massif range from 47% to 79% sunlit, and the app's 79.1% falls inside that range.

What we made up, and say so on screen: in rover mode only, rocks under 1.3 m and craters under 4 m across, which no NASA map shows. Every other height comes from a NASA map.

Tools and languages

JavaScript and HTML in the browser, with Three.js 0.169.0 for 3D. No build step and no server code: the site is static files on Cloudflare Pages, and it loads nothing from other hosts. Python (NumPy, tifffile) to download and cut the NASA maps and ray-cast the skylines. Node.js for the accuracy checks. Source code: https://github.com/ukasha167/lunar-landing-site-navigator (MIT licence).

SI use

The team came up with the idea and chose the design. Claude Code, an AI coding agent, wrote the code, the data scripts and the checks, and drew design sketches the team picked from. The team set the go/no-go rule and checked the results against JPL Horizons and NASA's sunlight map. Every source file says this in its header, and the README has a "Use of AI" section.
